deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German lecture or study notes on early Greek history. It continues the previous page, which ends with the Deucalion–Hellen genealogy of the Greek tribes. The page states:

(1) The Hellenic tribes (Dorians, Aeolians, Achaeans, Ionians) stayed distinct in language, customs and constitution through all later times.

(2) Foreign colonists also came from Egypt, Phoenicia and Asia Minor, dated 1600–1400 BC.

(3) First colony: Cecrops, c. 1550, from Sais in Lower Egypt to Attica. He laid the foundation of the citadel of Athens and introduced fixed marriage.

(4) Second colony: Danaus, c. 1500, from Upper Egypt. He settled at Argos in the Peloponnese.

(5) Cadmus, 1550, from Phoenicia to Boeotia. He built the citadel Cadmea, and through him the Greeks learned alphabetic writing.

(6) Fourth colony: Pelops, c. 1400, from Asia Minor (read as Mysia; the usual tradition says Phrygia or Lydia). He was expelled by the Trojan king Ilus and settled in Elis. The Peloponnese ('island of Pelops') is named after him.

The only numbers on the page are traditional dates BC. There are no derivations to reconstruct. The content and dates match the standard Göttingen textbook chronology of A. H. L. Heeren's ancient-history handbook (1799 ff.), which gives Cecrops 1550, Danaus 1500, Cadmus 1550 and Pelops 1400. This suggests these are notes from Heeren-style history lectures, my inference. The handwriting and content suggest they may not be by Gauss himself; possibly a family member's or a student's school notes were filed in the bundle.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.
Historically, these are traditional, mythographic dates with no factual basis. For comparison, the Parian Marble gives Cecrops c. 1582/1, Cadmus c. 1519/8 and Danaus c. 1511/0 BC.

Pelops' origin is usually given as Phrygia or Lydia (Sipylus), not Mysia, if 'Mysien' is the correct reading. Pelops is usually dated well after 1400 in ancient chronographers. The note simply reproduces a schoolbook scheme.

The ordinal enumeration is loose. The text counts Cecrops as 'the first' colony, Danaus as 'another', leaves Cadmus unnumbered, then calls Pelops the '4th'. This is consistent only if Cadmus is counted third.
The previous-page transcription says the Hellenes first lived in Thessaly and then moved to Thessaly. That looks like a transcription slip; Phthiotis or Parnassus is probably meant.

results.what: Traditional chronology of the oriental colonists of Greece (Cecrops, Danaus, Cadmus, Pelops)
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient chronographers (Parian Marble, Eusebius); textbook form in A. H. L. Heeren, Handbuch der Geschichte der Staaten des Alterthums (1799)

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely non-mathematical, routine history-lecture material reproducing standard early-19th-century textbook chronology. It may not even be in Gauss's hand. Nothing here bears on Gauss's mathematics.

checkable.asserts: The colony dates given (1550, 1500, 1550, 1400) fall within the stated immigration window 1600–1400 BC.
150 years separate Cecrops/Cadmus (1550) from Pelops (1400) in the notes' chronology.

transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'darin[?]' is uncertain in the image; the word after 'Zeiten' looks like 'darte'/'dort'. The sense is just 'remained distinguished'.

Line 5: 'Ihre Einwanderung[?] stellen[?]' is doubtful. The image looks more like 'Ihre Zeit kann man daraus/darum ... stellen zwischen 1600–1400', meaning one can place their time between 1600 and 1400.
'Klein-Asien' is written with 'Asien' corrected or added above the line (red-pencil marks); the reading is fine.
'Mysien[?]' fits the letter shapes ('Mysien'). Note that tradition usually says Phrygia/Lydia.
'Der Peloponnes, bekam von ihm den Namen' is confirmed.
The red pencil ticks on lines 1, 4 and 13 are later corrector's marks, not text.
